review:
I’ve put hundreds of hours into CS:GO over the years, so when CS2 finally dropped, I wanted to love every second of it. The reality? It’s a masterclass in gunplay wrapped in one of the most frustrating matchmaking environments in modern gaming. First off, the game looks and feels clean. The jump to Source 2 wasn't just a simple coat of paint maps like Inferno and Nuke actually look like modern games now without losing the clear lines of sight we need to hit headshots.

The volumetric smoke mechanics are easily the coolest thing Valve has done to tactical shooters in a decade. Being able to pop a grenade right into a smoke cloud to open a temporary line of sight, or watching smoke naturally flood into tight rooms and down staircases, completely changes how you play sites. It makes old, stale execute strategies feel fresh again.

We have to talk about it, because pretending it isn't happening ruins any real conversation about this game.

Premier mode right now, especially once you push past 15k CS Rating is an absolute mess. VAC Live was hyped up as this revolutionary AI anti-cheat that would cancel games the second someone started cheating, but in practice, it feels completely invisible. You will regularly run into blatant wallhackers, triggerbots, and full-on spinbots who shoot you through walls before you even round a corner.

3 out of 5 Stars not until the cheating issue is resolved.

# I DID NOT CHEAT. SO WHY AM I BEING PUNISHED FOR PLAYING COUNTER-STRIKE?

**NOT RECOMMENDED — THREE VACNET INCIDENTS, A 31-DAY COOLDOWN, AND ABSOLUTELY NO TRUST LEFT IN THIS SYSTEM.**

I love Counter-Strike. I genuinely do.

I've spent hundreds of hours playing this game, practicing my aim, learning maps, studying utility lineups, and improving my skills.

But after everything that has happened over the past few weeks, I'm seriously starting to question why I even bother.

**THREE VACNET INCIDENTS INVOLVING MY FRIENDS AND ME.**

And now, **I HAVE BEEN GIVEN A 31-DAY COOLDOWN FOR "IRREGULAR GAMEPLAY."**

Let me make one thing absolutely clear:

**I. DID. NOT. CHEAT.**

No aimbot. No wallhacks. No triggerbot. No cheating software.

I know what I did and didn't do on my own computer. I am not going to pretend that I'm unsure about whether I cheated.

I didn't.

## THREE INCIDENTS. HOW MANY MORE?

**October 11, 2026 — First incident**

We were playing Competitive Mirage. The score was 8–9 when VACnet cancelled the match.

One of my friends had performed a wallbang toward Kitchen from the B site after hearing audio cues.

Apparently, a legitimate wallbang was followed by a cancelled match.

We received cooldowns.

**October 14, 2026 — Second incident**

Another Competitive Mirage match.

This time, the score was 4–3 when VACnet cancelled it.

No unusual wallbangs. No crazy plays. Nothing that we could identify as suspicious.

Another incident. More cooldowns.

**October 23–24, 2026 — Third incident**

This time, it was MY turn.

Just **TWO DAYS** after my previous cooldown expired, my friends and I completed a match normally.

Then a yellow notification appeared.

**"IRREGULAR GAMEPLAY."**

And suddenly:

**31 DAYS OF COOLDOWN.**

My friends were penalized too.

**ARE YOU SERIOUS, VALVE?**

I waited for my previous punishment to expire, returned to the game, played normally, and got punished AGAIN.

What am I supposed to do now? Wait another month, come back, and hope the same thing doesn't happen?

## WHAT EXACTLY DID I DO WRONG?

During the third match, I made several plays that might look impressive or suspicious without context.

**1. A lucky headshot through smoke.**

I fired through smoke and happened to hit an enemy in the head.

That's called luck. It happens in Counter-Strike.

**2. An AWP collateral kill at Mid Doors.**

Two enemies lined up. I fired one bullet and killed both.

That's literally how the AWP works.

**3. A normal wallbang.**

Wallbangs are part of Counter-Strike. Players practice them. Professionals use them.

**4. Pre-aiming an enemy after seeing their shadow.**

I noticed an opponent's shadow before the opponent became visible.

So I aimed accordingly.

**SINCE WHEN IS USING INFORMATION PROVIDED BY THE GAME ITSELF CONSIDERED SUSPICIOUS?**

Am I supposed to ignore enemy shadows?

Am I supposed to intentionally miss shots through smoke?

Should I stop practicing wallbangs?

Should I apologize every time I hit a lucky shot?

**DO I HAVE TO PLAY WORSE JUST TO FEEL SAFE FROM ANOTHER COOLDOWN?**

I don't know which action, if any, caused VACnet to flag me. But I know I wasn't cheating.

## DON'T BELIEVE ME? WATCH THE EVIDENCE.

I'm not asking anyone to blindly trust a random Steam review.

I've uploaded the **FULL MATCH DEMO** and four separate gameplay clips.

Watch them. Examine my gameplay. Draw your own conclusions.

**FULL MATCH DEMO:**

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Sd35EuE3Osb2O_uxmGkH1M0m69IZdEQU/view?usp=drive_link

**CLIP 1 — Shadow-Based Pre-Aim:**

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1k6ErYgNM4KhlbLIp676vJF1XVInkp9XS/view?usp=drive_link

**CLIP 2 — Standard Wallbang:**

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ByXL7Bj998WBG8INU61OHVNqAjBYTqTB/view?usp=drive_link

**CLIP 3 — Lucky Headshot Through Smoke:**

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1v4V_iKs0g04gegNDNhdmfn2dYJV1Kziq/view?usp=drive_link

**CLIP 4 — AWP Collateral (Two Kills, One Shot):**

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jqWtNxtN1_SLvTBOyG45GtXPKXJsDgiV/view?usp=drive_link

**I AM WILLING TO HAVE MY ENTIRE MATCH REVIEWED.**

If you think something in my gameplay proves I cheated, tell me exactly what it is.

## AND NOW MY TRUST FACTOR IS AFFECTED TOO?

Before these incidents, my friends never received red Trust Factor warnings when queuing with me.

Now they do.

I cannot prove what caused this change, but the timing makes the entire situation even more frustrating.

Not only am I unable to play competitive matches, but my account now appears less trustworthy to my friends.

All while I know I have not cheated.

## VALVE, THIS IS UNACCEPTABLE.

I understand why Counter-Strike needs strong anti-cheat protection.

Nobody wants to play against cheaters.

**BUT WHAT ABOUT LEGITIMATE PLAYERS WHO GET FLAGGED INCORRECTLY?**

What are we supposed to do?

Sit quietly for 31 days?

Accept the punishment without questioning it?

Hope that someone at Valve eventually notices?

I've already contacted Valve and requested a manual review.

I provided my SteamID, match information, full demo, and gameplay clips.

**I WANT AN ACTUAL INVESTIGATION, NOT JUST AN AUTOMATED PUNISHMENT THAT I HAVE NO MEANINGFUL WAY TO CHALLENGE.**

I am not claiming that Valve has officially acknowledged these incidents as false positives.

But I am absolutely certain about one thing:

**I DID NOT CHEAT.**

And I should not have to spend an entire month away from a game I love because of a cooldown I believe was issued incorrectly.

The worst part isn't even the 31 days.

It's the feeling that I could return after the cooldown expires, play another completely normal match, hit another lucky shot, and end up right back here.

**HOW CAN I ENJOY A COMPETITIVE GAME IF I'M AFRAID OF PLAYING WELL?**

Counter-Strike is supposed to reward practice, game sense, reaction time, and skill.

It should not make legitimate players afraid of using those skills.

**VALVE, PLEASE REVIEW MY FULL DEMO AND INVESTIGATE ALL THREE INCIDENTS.**

**REMOVE MY 31-DAY COOLDOWN AND MY FRIENDS' INCORRECT PENALTIES IF YOUR REVIEW CONFIRMS THEY WERE WRONGFULLY ISSUED.**

I don't want special treatment.

I don't want cheaters to go unpunished.

I just want a fair system.

**I LOVE COUNTER-STRIKE, BUT I CANNOT RECOMMEND A GAME THAT CURRENTLY MAKES ME AFRAID TO PLAY IT.**

watch the evidence. i'm not asking anyone to blindly trust a random steam review. i've uploaded the **full match demo** and four separate gameplay clips. watch them. examine my gameplay. draw your own conclusions. **full match demo:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1sd35eue3osb2o_uxmgkh1m0m69izdequ/view?usp=drive_link **clip 1 — shadow-based pre-aim:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1k6erygnm4khlblip676vjf1xvinkp9xs/view?usp=drive_link **clip 2 — standard wallbang:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1byxl7bj998wbg8inu61ohvnqajbytqtb/view?usp=drive_link **clip 3 — lucky headshot through smoke:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1v4v_iks0g04gegndnhdmfn2dyjv1kziq/view?usp=drive_link **clip 4 — awp collateral (two kills, one shot):** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jqwtnxtn1_slvtboyg45gtxpkxjsdgiv/view?usp=drive_link **i am willing to have my entire match reviewed.** if you think something in my gameplay proves i cheated, tell me exactly what it is. ## and now my trust factor is affected too? before these incidents, my friends never received red trust factor warnings when queuing with me. now they do. i cannot prove what caused this change, but the timing makes the entire situation even more frustrating. not only am i unable to play competitive matches, but my account now appears less trustworthy to my friends. all while i know i have not cheated. ## valve, this is unacceptable. i understand why counter-strike needs strong anti-cheat protection. nobody wants to play against cheaters. **but what about legitimate players who get flagged incorrectly?** what are we supposed to do? sit quietly for 31 days? accept the punishment without questioning it? hope that someone at valve eventually notices? i've already contacted valve and requested a manual review. i provided my steamid, match information, full demo, and gameplay clips. **i want an actual investigation, not just an automated punishment that i have no meaningful way to challenge.** i am not claiming that valve has officially acknowledged these incidents as false positives. but i am absolutely certain about one thing: **i did not cheat.** and i should not have to spend an entire month away from a game i love because of a cooldown i believe was issued incorrectly. the worst part isn't even the 31 days. it's the feeling that i could return after the cooldown expires, play another completely normal match, hit another lucky shot, and end up right back here. **how can i enjoy a competitive game if i'm afraid of playing well?** counter-strike is supposed to reward practice, game sense, reaction time, and skill. it should not make legitimate players afraid of using those skills. **valve, please review my full demo and investigate all three incidents.** **remove my 31-day cooldown and my friends' incorrect penalties if your review confirms they were wrongfully issued.** i don't want special treatment. i don't want cheaters to go unpunished. i just want a fair system. **i love counter-strike, but i cannot recommend a game that currently makes me afraid to play it.** steamid64: **76561199230785615**

review:
Even though i've never played CSGO pre-CS2, i can totally understand why CS2 is such a downgrade from the old game, and even though i love this game from the bottom of my heart and want to reach high level in it, i cannot get over the feel of randomness and inconsistency within this game, so i will have to leave a negative review, but i wont just cry about obvious things such as VAC, i will list all and every concerns i do have for the game, so here goes nothing.
1. Subtick is bad, if you cannot go back to 64 or 128 tick, well, at least make sure it works as good as possible, because right now, as of November 2026 (3 years since the launch of the game) we still die behind walls, have worse hit registration than Counter Strike 1.6 (20+ years old game btw) and cannot hold angles without moving, which also created the wide swing meta, which is such a shame, because it kills the baseline which CSGO players learned and myself learned because i started the game with tutorials from CSGO and based my playstyle around them. Plus now, playing past 50ms ping is close to unplayable in a competitive scenario, it feels like CSGO at 120ms ping.
2. Fix movement, it's literally a single value in the engine, the initial velocity when starting a movement in any direction is much lower than in CSGO, which makes running and gunning way too effective, since the running accuracy penalty is directly related to your velocity, so you don't get punished enough for that like you did in CSGO, run and gun was a literal joke, so how did it become a meta ? How is it normal that you can get killed by a Silver running with an AK that just hits a lucky headshot while aiming at the ground ? As i said, its a single value to change and it should be fine.
3. Get rid of bullet variance on Sniper Rifles, for other guns, fine, i get why, but sniper rifles ? Come on buddy, pin point accuracy is the bread and butter of the AWP and Scout.
4. Why change the brightness system if in CSGO, all you had to do was boost your vibrance ? You're trying to make the game the same for everyone visually even though Counter Strike was always about customization ? Counter Strike itself is a modification of a game for God's sake.
5. Little to no new content, and when there is, it's either made by the community and bought by Valve, or it's the simplest thing ever and anyways, cheaters will flood it and talking about that.
6. Anticheat, i understand why in today's world its so hard to make a good anticheat, especially without crossing so many privacy borders, and id say the most recent VAC upgrade was pretty good, except, it can also flag legit players lol, so one time i bought a scout regularly in a Premier Dust 2 game and got cooldown 20h, hmm, yeah, weird. Oh and don't forget, closet cheaters still exist, full rage cheaters now just have a really hard time not getting caught, which is cool, but doesn't mean the fight is over yet.
7. Get rid of armor aim punch, so if you didn't know, yes, even if you have armor, you still take a slight aim punch effect, which is really low, but in a game where a pixel can make the difference between hitting your shot and missing badly, it has an impact on the gameplay. So, we buy kevlar to just reduce aim punch now ? Come on, blud, just remove that, it takes 5 minutes to do that.
8. Optimization, yeah, i know, its not the worst optimization that exists and yeah okay, a new game on a new engine will always take more resource, especially when the old game was made in an engine from 2003 but let's go back to the reason Valve implemented subtick. They said they can't put 128 tick matchmaking because the PCs of most of the playerbase are trash and can't handle, well first that was more than 10 years ago and i don't think it makes that large of a difference, especially when you see Valorant, which is 128 tick and has one of the best optimization ever for an E-Sports title, and also, if you give this reason, why optimize the new game so bad ? Because well, you just made the game harder to run and have a crappy netcode, like, come on, man, it's actually stupid that a 17 yo guy who started playing the game a year ago understands that better than dedicated grown adult developers for the biggest E-Sports franchise ever, or well, it could be the second one if things go like that for longer.
8. Flashbangs, why do they muffle you for so long ? That makes friendly flashes really annoying because you can't hear anything for longer if you get clipped by a flashbang remotely near you, sure it is more realistic BUT THAT GAME WAS NEVER MEANT TO BE REALISTIC, GOD DAMN IT. Why change somethIng that worked perfectly ? CS 1.6 flashes are too powerful, Source ones still a bit too much, and GO's flashes were literal perfection.
9. Put Cobblestone and Tuscan back, those a little rants and i know a Cobble remake could come back, or at least i've heard rumors about it, but hurry up, the Cache remake is a banger, so i know you guys have the potential to make good remakes for these two ones. Tuscan, i know is an old map, but if anything in the competitive scene, i think we need more variations in maps, and Tuscan, as ive studied it, could be a really refreshing map to play. For Cobble, base yourself on the pre-Halloween update version, and we should be fine.
10. The sticker revenues better get bigger for the next majors (Pro scene concern), have you seen how many smaller orgs turned their back on Counter Strike ? This is such a shame, because Counter Strike is supposed to be accessible to everyone, if they have the skill to compete at this level. But if the profitability is so low, orgs that don't have the financial capacity of Vitality, Falcons or various gambling platforms will either go bankrupt or just leave the game. Do we want a pro scene where only 10 teams will play the big tournaments ? Of course not ! Who didn't love watching Bad News Eagle, Apeks, Ence or Endpoint back in the day ? These were interesting teams to see climb up the ladder to reach majors and break expectations... But it seems like if nothing changes and Majors go the same way as the 2026 Cologne one did, it could mean that Pro Scene is GG.
11. The smokes, this is entirely subjective, some liked one ways back in CSGO, some hated them, i know it was a bug but think about it, BunnyHopping was also a bug originally and CS Devs said it themselves when they tried to remove it in CS2 (Tell a lot about their iq and understanding of the game lmfaoo), so why remove the CSGO smokes and not BunnyHop with this logic ? Also, for anyone saying that they didn't like one ways, i completely understand your opinion, all i have to say is that it was a skill check and promoted studying the map even further to find these one ways, because a lot of players forgot that but, to do these one ways, players like Monesy had to sit on offline maps for hours to actually find them.
Conclusion: This game should be the best and most balanced competitive shooter on the market as of now, but simply isn't, too many problems plague the game and turned it into wide swinging and brainless aggression simulator and the overall level of mechanics and intelligence of the community reflect just that, every day i see people reaching Level 10 Faceit when in CSGO, they were at best Level 6 or 7, that's not a coincidence. In all honesty, if Valorant wasn't an Hero Shooter and just a search and destroy game, i wouldve switched to it in seconds, but since there isn't really anything like CS and i love the game, i play it and try my best to get better at it everyday. But when the game is so unresponsive and inconsistent and the devs make it very clear that they are lazy and don't understand crap about the game and what its community wants, i cannot support it. To all the players that will read this, do not open cases, do not buy your skins from the Steam Marketplace and do not watch pro games, because the language that Valve speaks is revenues. So, Valve, please fix

review:
This new VACNet ban system is a joke.

Use an AWP or scout, hit a few good shots, and suddenly your gameplay gets flagged as irregular. Meanwhile, you can play against someone pre-firing every corner dropping 40+ kills and apparently that’s fine.

I’ve been playing CS for 10 years and in the past three months I’ve been flagged four times. I’m now up to a 31-day ban. At this point you basically have to stop playing the game or have multiple accounts to jump between.

If you’re going to use an AI system to automatically ban players you at least need to tell them why they were flagged. Was the aim considered suspicious? Is some piece of software triggering the system? Was it movement, input behaviour or something else entirely?

If these cases aren’t going to be reviewed by a human, players need some way of understanding what VACNet actually detected. Otherwise you get banned come back, have no idea what caused it, get flagged again, and the bans just keep getting longer.

I'm sad that they let this happen to my favourite competitive game. And I'm even sadder for all the players who are still willing to spend their money on skins and cases for a company that doesn't give a shit about your experience in their game as long as the money is flowing. I am very disappointed.

Dear Valve and Counter-Strike 2 Support Team,

I am writing to express my serious frustration and disappointment with the current punishment system and the way toxic behavior is handled in Counter-Strike 2.

How is it fair that I receive a 24-hour ban for killing a teammate, while that same teammate was repeatedly insulting me, verbally abusing me in Russian, and attempting to kick me from the match simply because I was playing the game my own way rather than following his personal demands?

Where was the moderation system when I was being verbally abused? Where are the consequences for players who use insults, harassment, intimidation, and toxic communication to ruin other players’ experiences?

Is the player who is being harassed expected to suffer the punishment, while the person provoking, insulting, and harassing others gets to continue playing without consequences?

I am not claiming that team killing should be acceptable. However, it is unacceptable for the punishment system to judge an incident without considering the circumstances, provocation, and harassment that led up to it.

I am requesting the following actions:

A proper review of my 24-hour ban, including the circumstances surrounding the incident.
An investigation into the abusive behavior and verbal harassment directed at me, including any available voice or text chat evidence.
Appropriate penalties for players who repeatedly harass, insult, and verbally abuse their teammates.
Improvements to the reporting and punishment system so that harassment and provocation are taken seriously, rather than focusing exclusively on the final reaction.
Equal treatment and fair protection for every player, regardless of their preferred playstyle or language.
One final message to the Counter-Strike 2 team:

Counter-Strike 2 is supposed to be a competitive team-based game built around skill, cooperation, and fair competition. It is not a dictatorship where one player gets to decide how everyone else must play, insult teammates, and abuse the kick system whenever someone refuses to follow their orders.

We enter this game to compete, improve, cooperate, and win — not to endure verbal abuse and then become the ones punished for reacting to it.

If Valve genuinely wants to maintain a healthy and professional gaming community, it must ensure that its punishment system protects all players and holds toxic individuals accountable.

I expect this case to be taken seriously, reviewed fairly, and addressed with a clear response.

Thank you for your time and attention.

Sincerely,
A Counter-Strike 2 Player

[h1]A Digital Love-Hate Relationship[/h1]

Counter-Strike 2 delivers the most contrasting emotions imaginable. On one hand, dropping into a random match introduces you to wonderfully eccentric strangers whose identities remain a total mystery—players who tape their microphones to their mouths to chant prayers or casually vent their life stories. 

Suddenly, the voice chat transforms into an impromptu stand-up comedy special, leaving you with an involuntary smile as hilarious, unscripted chaos unfolds. Executing a flawless site take with your team or pulling off a miraculous eco-round win simply wipes away all the stress of a long day.

[h2]The Other Side of the Coin[/h2]
[list]
[*]The smooth, nostalgic feel of the CS:GO era sometimes feels missing; the movement and overall pacing don't quite capture that exact old-school flavor.
[*]Let's not ignore the reality of cheaters still occasionally slipping into lobbies despite Prime matchmaking, forcing you to question whether you just got outplayed or out-hacked.
[/list]

[quote]
Yet, despite all its flaws, head-scratching moments, and hacker frustrations, jumping in after a long day to share laughs and build camaraderie makes it all worth it. It’s deeply flawed, utterly maddening, but undeniably magnetic.
[/quote]

[hr][/hr]

[i][b]Author's Note:[/b] The purpose of this review is simply to bring a smile to anyone reading it, highlighting the game's lighthearted and fun side while acknowledging its genuine quirks. If you look at my profile and notice this account only picked up Prime in early 2024, don't worry—I'm no stranger to the franchise, having logged plenty of hours across CS 1.6 and CS:GO on older accounts. Good games, everyone![/i]

review:
Let me introduce myself so you will get the feeling who is this review coming from. I started playing Counter Strike probably in 2003 or 2004 on the school PCs and in the local internet cafes. When I finally got PC with DSL connection in June 2006 the first game I bought was Counter Strike: Source and this was the exact moment when I created this Steam account. Later on Steam had some big database outage and all my hours recorded back in the days are lost so what you can see in my account now doesn't represent how many hours I spent in the game before CS:GO times. And then of course when CS:GO arrived it had many flaws, I didn't really start to play it until November 2014. Since then I played all the time, if not on this account then on another where I have 1k+ hours just playing with lower rank friends. I was so excited for CS2 - it was anticipated that it will have much more frequent updates, new interesting content, operations, better mechanics with subtick and all that stuff. We were told that CS:GO was lacking new nice things because of the "spaghetti code" that always meant breaking stuff and creating bugs whenever you touch it. CS2 supposed to be refactored game that makes all that issues gone. Guess what - it was all a lie. Things only got worse content-wise, subtick is a trash randomness and everybody wishes that 128 tick servers come back, and now they implemented some chicken eggs instead of things that players ask for - it's a complete slap in the face. We don't know what this is all for and who gives requirements to the devs, but that Product Owner should be replaced ASAP, the game was in the better state 3-4 years ago and earlier.

But I didn't even mention the worst thing that makes playing completely pointless. CHEATERS. There is no full version of VAC enabled in this game. Some auto-inputs are detected in some cases, but VERY rarely, and cheating such as wallhacking is fully allowed with no consequences. I know it first hand from the colleagues who just got so annoyed that they tried cheating themselves. It just revealed that every time when we thought "huh, that guy knows a lot", it was really just the wallhack and not the gamesense-like-a-pro players all the time. Playing faceit is now senseless as well. Cheat devs somehow have access to live data of all matches and you can literally turn on radar of every game in the browser on the 2nd screen (ie on the smartphone or 2nd monitor). Installing anticheat doesn't even secure anything as "cheats" can run on another machine and display what they want in the browser. I am suspecting that Valve devs participate in the share for being payed by players who buy these cheats because otherwise I don't see the reason why they can't patch the leaking server information. Oh and outside of faceit - you don't need this browser thing as all the information, every detail about every player on the server is stored locally on your RAM. Premier cheats use it like an open book. This could be patched easily as well. So Valve devs must somehow benefit from it that they keep it like that.

I can't recommend this game to anyone at this point. I will not play it again until internet will be flood over with the information that cheating problem is fixed, which I guess will never happen. This is it for me, about 23 years of playing Counter Strike and I am done.

⭐ RECOMMENDED: CS2 — A Masterpiece of Human Suffering

CS2 is genuinely one of the best games ever made. You launch it expecting a competitive shooter, but instead you get a psychological evaluation, an online casino, and a live demonstration of why humanity should never have discovered the internet.

The cheaters: Every third match feels like a job interview with someone who has a gaming chair sponsored by the devil himself. Bro is staring at walls, tracking enemies through seven dimensions, and still types "ez" after going 4–17. VAC is so effective that cheaters have time to get married, raise children, and teach their grandchildren how to use spinbot before receiving a ban.

The community: Absolutely beautiful. You miss one smoke and suddenly a 35-year-old Russian philosopher is explaining why your entire bloodline deserves execution. Teammates will flash you, block you, steal your weapons, and then report YOU for griefing. It's basically a family reunion, except everyone hates you and nobody brought a will.

review:
The game is completely free-to-play, and that, combined with the massive graphical upgrade, is the main reason for this positive review of CS2. Everything that came out after "Counter-Strike: Source" was absolute garbage to me, but CS2 finally looks up to date, costs nothing, and completely caught my attention visually.
Of course, the gameplay takes some getting used to. The movement feels a bit more sluggish at first, and this miserable sub-tick system causes occasional debates because it changes the whole feel of the game. It still leads to situations where shots don't register properly or you die even though you were already safely behind a wall on your own screen. But once you get used to the new rhythm, you realize what a modern masterpiece the game has become visually.
Then there is the endless cheater problem, where you just hope Valve will clamp down harder soon. People cheat way more subtly nowadays compared to the old days—using stuff like silent aim, legit bots, or soft aim, not to mention the config cheaters who abuse settings for an unfair advantage. New players even have to buy Prime just to get a rank. Luckily, I got Prime status for free because I’ve been around for over 10 years and experienced basically 5 to 10 different Counter-Strike versions. But let’s be honest: even Prime barely protects you from cheaters on the official servers these days, as Valve simply can't get a grip on their system. So you only have the advantage because, as a veteran, you didn't have to burn money for it.
With all the hype around skins and loot boxes, they are really trying to milk people for their money these days. Looking back at the early days of CS 1.0, you still remember downloading skins for free from fan homepages. Fortunately, you don't have to participate in this modern cash grab to still have fun on the server thanks to the new engine and graphics.
In the end, I recommend it purely for the new visuals and because it's free. As a veteran, you definitely need thick skin because of the cheaters, but after the first 20.9 hours, the graphics simply hooked me again.

CS2 is honestly one of the best competitive FPS games ever made. The gunplay, movement, mechanics, strategy, and overall competitive atmosphere are what keep millions of players coming back. No other game quite captures the same feeling of landing a perfect headshot, clutching a 1v4, or winning a hard-fought match with your team. It's a game that rewards skill, patience, teamwork, and thousands of hours of practice.

However, it's genuinely disappointing that even after all these years, cheating is still an issue. Nothing ruins an otherwise great competitive experience faster than running into someone using hacks. You can improve your aim, learn every smoke lineup, master every map, and spend countless hours developing your skills, only to have a cheater ruin the entire match.

CS2 has the potential to be the ultimate competitive FPS, but until anti-cheat becomes more effective and cheaters are dealt with properly, the experience will never be as good as it deserves to be.

A legendary game, an incredible community, and unfortunately, a problem that just refuses to disappear.

review:
INDUSTRIAL SOCIETY AND ITS FUTURE

Introduction

1. The Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for the human race. They have greatly increased the life-expectancy of those of us who live in “advanced” countries, but they have destabilized society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to indignities, have led to widespread psychological suffering (in the Third World to physical suffering as well) and have inflicted severe damage on the natural world. The continued development of technology will worsen the situation. It will certainly subject human beings to greater indignities and inflict greater damage on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater social disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased physical suffering even in “advanced” countries.

2. The industrial-technological system may survive or it may break down. If it survives, it MAY eventually achieve a low level of physical and psychological suffering, but only after passing through a long and very painful period of adjustment and only at the cost of permanently reducing human beings and many other living organisms to engineered products and mere cogs in the social machine. Furthermore, if the system survives, the consequences will be inevitable: There is no way of reforming or modifying the system so as to prevent it from depriving people of dignity and autonomy.

3. If the system breaks down the consequences will still be very painful. But the bigger the system grows the more disastrous the results of its breakdown will be, so if it is to break down it had best break down sooner rather than later.

4. We therefore advocate a revolution against the industrial system. This revolution may or may not make use of violence; it may be sudden or it may be a relatively gradual process spanning a few decades. We can’t predict any of that. But we do outline in a very general way the measures that those who hate the industrial system should take in order to prepare the way for a revolution against that form of society. This is not to be a POLITICAL revolution. Its object will be to overthrow not governments but the economic and technological basis of the present society.

5. In this article we give attention to only some of the negative developments that have grown out of the industrial-technological system. Other such developments we mention only briefly or ignore altogether. This does not mean that we regard these other developments as unimportant. For practical reasons we have to confine our discussion to areas that have received insufficient public attention or in which we have something new to say. For example, since there are well-developed environmental and wilderness movements, we have written very little about environmental degradation or the destruction of wild nature, even though we consider these to be highly important.

review:
Counter Strike 2...

I absolutely love this game; having played tons of fps games across many different platforms I can say that the Counter Strike franchise is my personal favorite for sure and it's not even close. Having only played CS2 myself I cannot speak for the other versions of the game (which from what I hear were better in some ways) but everything about the game CS:GO as a whole is perfect to me.

If you are looking to chill and have fun Counter Strike 2 has game modes and custom maps / lobbies that are well made and enjoyable - and also if you are looking to have a decent chance at losing your sanity and going absolutely ballistic you can also do it on CS2 as well with their more competitive game modes. Both the more casual and the more competitive game modes are tons of fun regardless of the capability they both have to make someone want to destroy their whole gaming setup! The sheer satisfaction of the game will keep you coming back for more time and time again.

The weapons and maps in this game are very well made and highly thoughtful; the maps actually make sense and have features or places on them that feel like they were actually designed to support pvp and the infinite combination of things that can happen. The same goes for the weapons, everything is pretty balanced and the meta feels more like a suggestion; people can do very well with just about any weapon and I've seen it time and time again, but still an AK or M4 is the top pick for most.

I would 100% recommend Counter Strike 2 to anyone who enjoys player vs player fps games, but I can say that the game is fairly difficult starting off. There's a lot of little things to learn and tips here and there that you'll end up getting along the way - so the start of the game will be a little painful until you get used to it. Once you get comfortable with the game it will stand out as one of the best if not the best competitive experiences you can have at the higher level of play. Nothing beats the feeling of a good match or a huge clutch or play and almost passing out due to your heart wanting to leave your body and your adrenaline soaring through the roof.

The Counter Strike atmosphere is amazing, the major events and tournaments are actually a blast to watch and the multiple pro scenes around the globe are interesting to follow and keep up with the players and teams. The weapon skin and case system are also nice to get into and actually have entire markets based around them. All in all once you dive in a little bit to the game and the stuff around it you start to enjoy the game a lot more and it will make you significantly better.

I love you Gabe Newell - Thank you for making this beautiful game and the CS:GO franchise.

10/10 Game.

50/50 % Chance of Pure Misery or Pure Fun

Always 100% Glory.

review:
CS2 is easily one of my favorite FPS games. I love that it comes down to pure aim, skill, and teamwork instead of relying on a bunch of abilities. The maps are great, directional audio is solid, and I love the whole skin market, even if some of the prices are absolutely insane. Also, Counter-Strike has by far my favorite esports scene. Watching the Majors is honestly just as fun as playing the game sometimes.

My biggest regret is never getting to experience CS:GO. I knew about it growing up, but I didn't have a PC and was too busy playing COD. Looking back, I really wish I'd just tried running it on some shitty laptop. I've heard CS:GO had better gunplay and spray patterns, but I actually like how difficult CS2 is. Makes getting better at the game that much more satisfying.

Now, the cheating. Oh, where do I even start? Nothing better than playing a game that's supposed to be all about skill, only to get absolutely shit on by some loser who apparently needs third-party software to move his mouse for him. I fucking hate how infested this game is with cheaters. It's genuinely embarrassing how bad it can get, especially for a game this big.

Still love CS2 though. Just wish I could enjoy it without having to wonder if the guy on the other team is the next donk or just another idiot with cheats.

Extremely negative impressions of this game.

First, I completely disagree with this whole skins thing. It's gambling addiction. The game pushes you to spend more and more money. On top of that, you can really feel how many cheaters are in the game.

The interesting part is that I have a top-tier PC and a 480 Hz monitor, which really does give an advantage in the game. I'm from a region where my ping was around 100, and now I play with an average ping of 20. Because of that, I do pretty well in Competitive and in regular matches. I'm just an ordinary working guy who plays in the evenings and on weekends, and sometimes I play well.

But after a year of playing, almost 600 hours, I got hit with a low Trust Factor. I don't act toxic in chat and I don't insult anyone. So the only conclusion I can draw is that it's because of how I play. Yes, a couple of times I had over 40 kills, and quite often over 30. But that's no reason to give me a low Trust Factor.

Now, when I play with friends, we get matched against blatant cheaters and it's impossible to play. There is no clear way to get back to normal matchmaking, and playing with a low Trust Factor is simply impossible. I don't want to ruin the game for my friends. It's just a terrible feeling.

I really don't recommend it.

review:
I spent over 1000 hours in this game. Master Guardian rank here. I had wonderful experiences, met some great people and took a keen interest in the development of CS. But I can not recommend this game, even though I'd like to. Here's why and I ask you to take a moment to read this comment, because you may be the next victim.

I took a break from gaming for over a year and when I wanted to come back it turned out that someone hacked my Steam account and stole all my items. And these weren’t just any items (an AWP with a PashaBiceps sticker, a cool knife, tons of crates and more). You get it? The account had been inactive for over a year and suddenly someone dug up login data. BTW I’m careful about online security — I’ve never shared my login information with anyone, anywhere. Thieves changed the email address associated with my account without sending any notification about attempted change to my email address. How is that possible? After contacting Steam Support I got my account back, but no items.

It seems that the cases one has heard about have affected me as well; a Steam employee searches for accounts that appear to be inactive in order to take them over and steal their content. The thief initially logged in from various addresses, but after a while apparently gained confidence and was logging in from a single location — Chicago, USA. There are logs for that. Despite my best efforts Steam support refused to return my stolen goods. And since I can't ask for justice, I can at least write this comment.

Take this as a warning: if you take a longer break from CS, you might lose everything you've worked to achieve and paid real money for. No security measures will help you because this looks like an inside job by Steam employees who steal people's accounts, bypassing any security protocols, and go unpunished.

Shame on you, Steam.

Farewell, CS community.

1/10 — The Hackers Have Better Anti-Cheat Than the Developers
This game somehow managed to achieve an incredibly impressive feat – the actual enemy team isn’t the biggest problem here. The real monster is the anti-cheat.
Every single match is a competition of cheaters to see who can cheat more – wallhacks, aimbots, impossible tracking, headshots through walls – you name it, and at this point, I’m not even surprised. I’m not asking “how can they do this?” – I’m begging “how long are they going to let this happen?”
The very fact that the game’s “developers” allow this to happen is part of the issue, though
It’s wild how fast they could implement new skins, bundles, battle passes, events and other assorted cash grabs, but apparently, detecting a player who can spin around 5 times per second and wipe out an entire team while invisible through walls is too hard for their tiny team of developers to handle.
I can spend hours upon hours upon hours upon hours dedicated to improving my aim, learning the map, discovering new strategies and playing the game as it is supposed to be played – only for someone with a fresh account and a cheat to come into my lobby and turn it into a glorified target practice. I will report them, receive my prize of an empty “report received” message and pray that the next match won’t be another round of Hackerman Simulator 2026.
But what’s worse is that cheating in this game – and the lack of anti-cheat measures – destroy the game from the inside. The very premise of a competitive FPS is ruined when it’s possible to simply install a better cheat. Why would players invest time and money into the game if they can simply “download miracle cheat 3.0” and become the best player in the world?
The developers could have solved this problem in the past, but instead, they give us empty speeches about “community reports” and “dedicated servers”, giving us the same tired answers over and over again:
Hackers appear → players complain → devs promise action → nothing meaningful changes → hackers come back.
 It’s not funny anymore. The competitive FPS genre revolves around trust – and this single fact has been understood by cheat creators from day one. This development team, however, apparently does not have a brain, and that is a serious problem. The enemy team isn’t even the problem.At this point, the hackers aren’t cheating – they’re testing the quality of the anti-cheat and the dedication of the developers. Good gunplay, potentially fun gameplay, ruined by the feeling that I am playing the game against not opponents, but an army of script Kiddies who enjoy cheating. Will not be purchasing any time or items from this dev team until they show some dedication to fixing the game.

review:
A 20-Year-Old Game Still Waiting to Grow Up

So, it's finally my turn to write a review, and for some reason, I don't think I have anything positive to say.

I'm an amateur gamer, but even I can see some of the biggest problems with this game. Let's start with the three major ones.

1. Waiting Simulator 2

The waiting. God, the waiting.

You queue for a match, someone leaves, and suddenly you're stuck waiting another two minutes. Then comes the timeout vote, so naturally, you get to wait even longer. And don't even get me started on the complete absence of a surrender button.

Why? Seriously, why?

When a match has an obvious outcome, why force everyone to sit through it? Just give us a surrender system similar to Valorant's. If someone on your team leaves for 1 min, two votes should be enough to surrender. If the entire team is still present, require a majority vote (3 out of 5).

Introduce harsher penalties for leavers and make the remaining players' lives less miserable. It's not rocket science.

But apparently, keeping trolls and AFK players in the game is more important than respecting everyone's time. After all, that's potentially one more customer who might buy a skin, right?

2. Cheaters: The Unwanted Teammates

Things have improved somewhat with the latest changes, but there's still plenty of work to do.

One thing I'd love to see is a proper trust-based reporting system. Players who consistently submit legitimate reports should gradually gain more credibility, making their reports carry more weight than those of players who report everyone who kills them.

And yes, I'll use Riot as an example again. I might be one of Valorant's biggest haters, but there's one thing I genuinely respect: a community that actively wants cheaters gone rather than treating them as just another part of the game.

3. Two Decades of Development, Yet Somehow Still Regressing

This is probably my biggest disappointment.

After more than 20 years, you'd expect meaningful gameplay improvements. Instead, we've got a handful of changes, some questionable decisions, and mechanics that somehow feel worse than they did in CS 1.6 and CS: Source.

What happened to improving recoil, fixing the notorious backtracking problem, and refining movement mechanics? Instead, we got bunny hopping that's roughly 100 times harder and less rewarding. The one original and fun mechanic for valve games and they ruined it.

There are millions of videos demonstrating these issues, yet they continue to be treated like minor inconveniences rather than actual problems.

One mechanic that makes my balls boil is how movement affects shooting accuracy. Even the slightest movement or a jump can send your bullet trajectory flying 30–40 degrees away from where you're aiming. Seriously? Even with Parkinson's, I'd struggle to miss by that much. A much more reasonable deviation would be 1–3 degrees, not whatever the hell this is.

At this point, the game feels less like a shooter and more like a movement simulator. Winning gunfights is increasingly about who's better at wiggling back and forth, mastering movement timings, and knowing the exact millisecond to stop moving before shooting, rather than who's actually better at aiming and shooting. Congratulations, you've mastered the art of standing still.

And don't get me started on unscoped sniper shots occasionally flying so far off-screen that you'd think the bullet was trying to leave the server.

Then there's the backtracking issue. As far as my experience goes, the two competitive shooters where dying after you've already made it behind cover is particularly noticeable are CS2 and Valorant. Even Team Fortress 2, another Valve game, doesn't suffer from it nearly as severely. It's not completely absent, but it's nowhere near as frustrating.

These are fundamental gameplay issues that should have been addressed years ago, not problems we should still be discussing in 2026.

Final Thoughts

If you've just started playing CS2, you probably won't notice most of these problems. But after hundreds or thousands of hours, you start noticing the same issues over and over again. And when you see the developers adding chickens while barely addressing the fundamental problems, you begin to wonder where their priorities actually lie.

At this point, CS2 feels less like a competitive shooter and more like a stock market or an NFT marketplace with a shooting minigame attached.

And honestly, it's a shame. If only the Call of Duty developers had been smart enough not to turn their game into an unnecessarily bloated mess, we could have had something much more interesting: highly customizable weapons, impressive graphics, and an esports scene where players could copy professional players' builds and play styles.

But no.

We got chickens.

Hooray! 🐣

review:
I've been playing Counter-Strike for many years, and CS:GO will always be my favorite game of all time. Across multiple Steam accounts, I've probably accumulated around 8,000 hours or more in CS:GO and another 2,000 hours in CS2. Since CS2 has replaced CS:GO, it's naturally become one of my most-played and favorite games.

That being said, I'm disappointed to say that I still think CS:GO felt much better overall. There's just something missing from CS2. In my opinion, the subtick system is a failure and often feels worse than what we had before. I also believe removing the in-game community server browser was a terrible decision.

That's not to say CS2 doesn't have its redeeming qualities, because it certainly does. I love the new smoke mechanics, and I appreciate how much more consistent grenade jump throws are without the need for binds, especially for newer players. The menus look much better and are easier to navigate, the game obviously looks and sounds better, and there are plenty of new settings that are much easier to access without having to use the console.

I don't think people should stop downloading or giving CS2 a chance. You can be sure I'll always keep coming back to it. Every time I launch the game and play a few matches, I have a great time. However, I can't help but feel that the game that replaced CS:GO, my favorite game of all time, should play and feel a little better than it currently does.

That's why I'm leaving a negative review. Not because I want to turn people away from the game, but because I genuinely believe the developers can do better, and they've shown in the past that they're capable of it.

In fact, it was we who were penalized: despite having overcome such unfavorable odds, we received a 20-hour ban.

I earnestly implore Valve’s personnel to recognize a fundamental truth: they cultivate one of the most devoted player communities in the world, yet their treatment of it suggests a profound indifference to its welfare.

review:
Counter-Strike 2 is a monumental visual and technical overhaul of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, preserving the legendary tactical gameplay while modernizing the platform on Valve’s Source 2 engine.

What Works
Sub-Tick Architecture & Shooting: The moving past 64-tick/128-tick server limits means input response, shooting, and grenade throws execute instantly regardless of tick rate, making gunplay feel razor-sharp once adapted.

Dynamic Volumetric Smoke: Smokes now interact dynamically with lighting, bullets, and HE grenades. Blowing a temporal hole through a smoke wall with a grenade creates entirely new tactical dynamics and outplay opportunities.

Source 2 Visuals & Audio: Overhauled maps feature realistic PBR materials, clear reflections, improved lighting, and readable sightlines. The directional audio rework significantly improves sound localization.

Quality-of-Life Upgrades: Features like weapon refunds during buy phases, customizable loadout menus, and a transparent Premier ranking ladder streamline the competitive experience.

Room for Improvement
Anti-Cheat Concerns: Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC) still struggles to consistently filter out cheaters in high-ELO Premier matches compared to third-party platforms like FACEIT.

Content Parity: Missing legacy game modes, custom community map features, and server browser integrations from CS:GO are still being built back out.

Optimization & Frame Pacing: Higher hardware requirements mean lower-end PCs may experience performance dips or frametime spikes compared to legacy CS:GO.

The Verdict
CS2 lays an exceptional technical foundation for the next decade of competitive FPS games. While it launched with some content gaps, its core dynamic systems and graphical polish deliver the premier tactical shooter experience available today.

review:
CS2 has become inseparable from an item economy that I believe makes the surrounding experience increasingly hostile to players.

After nearly two decades of collecting, I lost my inventory to a coordinated scam involving fake FACEIT software and someone impersonating Steam Support. I was manipulated into authorizing the trades myself. Steam's response was that the items could not be restored.

What troubles me is the system surrounding this. CS2 items have real monetary value, can be traded between users, and have helped create an ecosystem of third-party marketplaces and phishing opportunities. Valve collects fees from this market, yet its own policy leaves scam victims bearing the loss even when deception is central to what happened.

Steam explicitly warns that its employees will never contact users through chat to investigate accounts or request item verification. Why, then, is impersonation so easy to exploit? Blocking the display name “Steam Support” alone wouldn't solve the problem, but stronger impersonation detection, clearer warnings, and better safeguards around suspicious trades are basic expectations for a platform that facilitates valuable digital transactions.

The wider economy deserves scrutiny, too. Research has repeatedly found an association between loot-box spending and problem gambling. When randomized cosmetic items, scarcity, resale value, and third-party trading converge, this stops feeling like a harmless cosmetic system and starts resembling a speculative market attached to a video game.

And what does the game itself offer in return? In my view, CS2 feels stale and dated, with too little meaningful innovation in features and mechanics to justify the importance placed on its surrounding economy.

Valve has built an enormous ecosystem around virtual items. I don't believe its safeguards and accountability have kept pace with the value it has encouraged players to place in them.

I'm no longer willing to recommend CS2 or support an ecosystem where the items can become more consequential than the game, while the consequences of a successful scam fall overwhelmingly on the victim.

I was playing Wingman with my friend, and 6 rounds in, the match got cancelled. Apparently, he was flagged by VAC. He was suspended for 20 hours. Me queuing up with him also got me suspended for 20 hours. On top of the suspension, I've lost all of my XP I've gained this week, and I think my rank got negatively affected.

I know for a fact that my friend isn't cheating. I know that it's also okay to make mistakes. What's not okay, though, is to think you're 100% right, which you admittedly do by not letting us appeal.

This isn't how you deal with cheaters. You should, at minimum, permanently ban cheaters. No wonder your game has such a large cheating problem when you let cheaters back into the wild 20 hours later.

And this is how you treat paying customers, who've done nothing wrong? Will we get compensation for this? ...Yeah we will, it'll probably be a larger suspension or an outright ban.

Valve is just not a serious company, despite how many times they're called "based". They just shoot themselves less in the foot than other companies.

review:
While many people complain about cheating, and love to falsely accuse others, I have experienced very little cheating. The game is mechanically solid. It is accessible, easy to learn, hard to master, has a robust player base, and is fun to experiment with different strategies.
The problem is that the developer is keen on soiling and exploiting a legacy of quality with unpleasant gimmicks, which honestly, seem to be born from an uninspired mind. 
Abandoning realism in character design, changing spray patterns, and removing popular official maps is corporatism at its worst.
Removing single plant bomb game type was the single most personally aggravating decision Valve made with Counter-Strike. 
The second most was taking CS:GO, which I paid for, removing it from my library and replacing it with "Free to Play" CS2 which was a downgrade in most everyway, all while expecting me to pay another $15 to be prime enabled. It's obnoxiously greedy. They already are making a fortune with their market system. 
Now, they have introduced a non-optional "Big Head" mode in casual. The entire concept flies in the face of what Counter-Strike is. Counter-Strike is about prediction and repeatability. I, frankly, would play Office with no changes to the map or gameplay into eternity, because the it's fun. The changes aren't.
I will continue to play CS2, but eventually they will grind me down to have such a distain that it'll be uninstalled.
Long live the chuds.

review:
CS2 has honestly become one of the most frustrating games I have ever played. It feels less like a competitive game and more like a ragebait simulator where the game keeps finding new ways to piss you off. You can play perfectly for several rounds and then suddenly everything goes wrong. Your teammates stop communicating, people start trolling, your shots feel completely inconsistent and somehow the enemy always seems to know exactly where you are. Even when you know someone is probably just better than you, the amount of suspicious plays you see makes you question everything. You can literally watch someone prefire a position they had no reason to know you were holding and then do it again the next round. At some point you stop asking whether you are playing badly and start asking whether the match is even fair.

The hacker problem makes it even worse. I know not every good player is cheating and not every suspicious player is actually a hacker, but there are way too many matches where something just feels completely off. You will see people tracking through walls, instantly snapping onto heads, pre firing the exact position you are in and doing things that are extremely difficult to explain. The worst part is when you are already having a bad game and then you run into someone who seems to be using cheats. Now the entire match becomes pointless because you are spending more time wondering whether the other team is legit than actually enjoying the game. You report them, finish the match and then queue again hoping the next game will be normal. Sometimes it is, sometimes it is not. That should not be normal for a competitive shooter this big.

The matchmaking experience can also be absolutely horrible. You can have a decent game one moment and then the next match feels like you have been thrown into a completely different universe. Teammates refuse to use microphones, someone disconnects, someone starts fighting with their own team and somehow you are still expected to take the match seriously. Then you lose and your rating takes the hit even though half the problems were completely outside your control. CS2 can make you feel like you are being punished for simply trying to play the game. You start another match thinking this one will be better and before you know it you are angry again. That constant cycle of queueing, getting frustrated, losing and queueing again is exactly why the game feels like it is designed to ragebait you.

What makes all of this even more annoying is that CS2 actually has an amazing foundation. The gunplay, maps, economy and competitive gameplay are still the reason people keep coming back. That is also why the problems are so much more frustrating. People are not angry because they hate Counter Strike. They are angry because they genuinely like the game and want it to be better. After putting hundreds of hours into it, the last thing you want is to feel like your matches are being ruined by hackers, terrible teammates, questionable matchmaking and endless frustration. CS2 can still produce some incredible games, but it can also produce some of the most miserable gaming sessions imaginable. At this point you finish a match and instead of thinking about how much fun you had, you are sitting there wondering why you even queued in the first place.

review:
I installed Counter-Strike 2 to experience competitive tactical shooting. Instead, I received a 24/7 psychological evaluation conducted by 9-year-olds with gaming chairs worth more than my electricity bill.

The matchmaking system is incredible. It consistently places me against people who appear to have been genetically engineered in a laboratory to click heads. Meanwhile, my bullets travel through enemies like I'm shooting them with legally registered air.

The hit registration is so advanced that sometimes even the developers don't know where my bullets went. Truly revolutionary technology.

The community is absolutely wonderful. Every match feels like a United Nations emergency meeting where everyone has Tourette's and a microphone from 2007.

The economy system is fantastic. I spend $4,750 on an AK-47 just to get immediately deleted by a man named xX_Daddy_Destroyer_Xx holding a Desert Eagle.

And the cheaters? Absolutely breathtaking. Some players have such incredible game sense that they can detect my location through three walls, two buildings, and possibly my childhood trauma.

I've lost friends, gained enemies, developed trust issues, and learned 14 different languages of profanity.

Final verdict:

review:
Terrible anticheat experience, had to quit the game.

Although the gameplay loop is pretty fun, it is practically unplayable for me, and VALVe essentially forced me to quit the game. 

A few weeks ago, I received a VACnet cooldown for 24 hours for "suspicious gameplay", despite not having cheated at all. For those unaware, VACnet is the server side anticheat which monitors gameplay and flags behaviors that may indicate cheating. I quickly contacted support, submitted a detailed ticket explaining the situation, and attached my match's demo file, along with an analysis of my gameplay. After 24 hours, I could play the game again, and after a few quick matches, I was yet again placed in cooldown, this time for 7 days. This was very frustrating, and I updated my existing ticket, since something was clearly very wrong here. No response was received.

On the same day, I found a reddit thread of others complaining about similar unexpected cooldowns, which made me think this was potentially a large scale bug. An admin replied to the thread and requested emails to an address in case people thought they were falsely put on cooldown. Sent an email, no update, and no changes were made to my account. I had to wait out the week myself. In this time, the update introducing the rush game mode and pets was introduced, which was pretty huge, and I had to miss out on that due to VALVe's incompetency.

After waiting out the cooldown, I was quite excited to log onto the game and check things out. I played a couple rush matches, and then hopped onto competitive, only to get a VACnet cooldown of 7 days again. I am typing this review out while still under this cooldown. Extremely frustrated. Support does nothing, the dev team does not care enough to fix this major issue.

Now I have no choice other than to quit the game entirely. Thank you, VALVe.

I’m primarily a Valorant player, so going into Counter-Strike 2, I honestly didn't quite get why people are so obsessed with this game. The movement dynamics and gunplay feel completely different, and coming from a tactical shooter with unique agent abilities, CS2 takes some getting used to.

That being said, once you put some time into it, the game is actually pretty decent. Here is my breakdown of what stands out:

Stunning Visual Overhaul: Visually, the jump to Source 2 is impressive. The lighting, water effects, clean map textures, and sub-tick mechanical feel make the game look and feel top-notch for a modern competitive shooter.

Toxicty & Community Realities: Let’s be real—the community isn't exactly the most polite group out there. But then again, expecting a soft-spoken, hyper-friendly lobby in high-stakes competitive FPS titles is almost impossible anyway. Toxicity comes with the territory in this genre, whether you are playing CS2 or Valorant.

Core Gameplay Experience: Strip away the toxic voice chat, and at its core, CS2 is a super solid, crisp tactical shooter. The utility lineups, smoke physics, and pure aim mechanics offer a steep learning curve that rewards raw precision and map awareness.

Overall, while it might not completely pull me away from maining Valorant, CS2 is a genuinely good game that lives up to its legendary predecessor—even if its player base keeps you on your toes!

review:
Counter‑Strike is, at its core, a genuinely fun and addictive game. The fast-paced action, the focus on teamwork, and the satisfaction of improving your aim and game sense make it a title that keeps you coming back. Whether you’re playing casually with friends or trying to climb the ranks, the game delivers a competitive experience that few shooters can match.

However, the game also suffers from several frustrating issues. One of the biggest problems is how overly sensitive the cooldown system is. It’s understandable that the developers want to prevent griefing, but the current system punishes players far too easily. Something as simple as vote‑kicking too many players—even when the kicks are justified—can result in a cooldown. This makes the system feel unfair and punishes normal players for using features that are built into the game.

These cooldowns can interrupt your momentum, ruin your session, and make the game feel more restrictive than it should be. When you’re trying to enjoy a match and suddenly get locked out for something minor, it takes away from the fun.

Overall, Counter‑Strike is a great game with strong gameplay and a loyal community, but the cooldown system desperately needs improvement. If the developers can make it less sensitive and more balanced, the experience would be much smoother and far less frustrating.

I made friends on here, and it definitely has its fun moments, especially when you do end up in a game that seems fair and cheater free. But in the end, I just can motivate myself to play something where cheating is so prevalent.

review:
CS:GO was better by far. Three years have passed since release, and we still aren't even close to the level of CS:GO. In fact, CS2 is in an even worse state in every possible way: cheaters, clunky gameplay, case-farming bots — the game has completely lost its soul and colors. The devs clearly don't care anymore. At this point, the entire game is carried by the community:

Maps? Made by the community.
Skins? Made by the community.
Anticheat? Handled by the community and third-party platforms.

Yet Valve still doesn't care about the players. They shake up and crash the market whenever they feel like it, ignore feedback, and give us nothing in return. Right now, CS2 isn't a game built to bring players joy — it's just a pure money-printing machine for Valve.

CS:GO felt alive. We had Operations, missions, and actual content. Now, CS2 is nothing more than a soulless FACEIT Elo / rank grind. Valve is pouring 100% of their time and passion into Deadlock, while CS2 is left completely empty — yet somehow overflowing with cheaters and bots.

The worst part? Me and millions of others will keep playing anyway, simply because there is no real alternative. Deep down, I still hope for a miracle — that someday Valve will finally remember CS2 exists. Until then... I just want CS:GO to come back.

review:
As a long term, multi-decade CS community member with over 5000 hours in CS:GO / CS2, I regretfully recommend against this game.

In an effort to combat cheaters, the developers have implemented new anti-cheat paramaters that are having adverse and unintended conesquences. Two members of our team - who aren't cheaters - have been effectively shadow banned from the game, with VAC ascribing to them negative 'Trust Factors'. It now takes our team 20+ minutes for matchmaking to que us into a game; which now consists predominately of other shadow-banned / low-trust factor players. 

Additionally, earlier this week one of our teammates triggered a 20 hour VAC cooldown for our whole team. Despite this, nobody on our team was found to be cheating, and yet the low-trust factor remains. 

In our recent matchamaking for 3 games, total playtime over 3 games was ~65 minutes, the wait time for queing in a restricted lobby was ~75 minutes. This new system is punitive and punishes skilled players, and has such a negative impact on matchmaking that if not corrected it will regress further and drive players away from the game.

Valve is acting like ruthless cops who hand out brutal, groundless punishments while refusing to state any specific charges or facts. Why do they behave like this? Because they simply want to, and because they can.

I can only view this as total contempt for me as a customer who paid real money for a Prime status, spent the most precious currency in life - my time - along with electricity and personal energy, only to receive this kind of "gratitude" in return. Submitting polite appeal tickets led nowhere, just automated dead ends and zero dialogue, while real cheaters keep playing unbothered. Until this completely unfounded ban is lifted, this negative review stays as a reminder of their corporate arrogance, but the moment a deserved amnesty is granted, I will gladly change it to positive.

review:
I don't exaggerate when I say I love this game, I have played CS since 1.6 and it has always been my go to game when I wanted to play with friends. I have pre-ordered CS:GO in closed beta, I was there when they brought skins, I was there when the first operation dropped, I was there when the first major for this game was played.

I'm not telling all these to get your eyes teary or stir up your emotions, I'm telling these to emphasize I really love this game and I was playing it all of its lifetime. But today I uninstalled it. Because this game is absolutely in shambles, not only do they fail to ban cheaters, but they also end up punishing you. 

I have never cheated in my life, even today if you wanted me to download cheats I don't know how to do it, I haven't used voice chat more than 3 times a game on average for the last year. Yet the game says my trust factor is too low, and I get thrown into a hellhole with all the misfits and cheaters whenever I try to queue up premier matchmaking. The game doesn't even ban hackers for hacking, yet it has no hesitation punishing their loyal players. Because you got reported a bunch of times for who knows, maybe playing good, maybe not doing something the team says, maybe even not responding to chat banter, you get placed into the quarantine zone and your experience is ruined.

And I don't want to install Windows 11 or pay a monthly fee to some third party site to play the free game I enjoy playing. review:
More Than Just a Game.

Counter-Strike is not just a game. It's an experience, a passion, and for many of us, a part of our lives.

There is something truly special about this game. Every match tells a different story. Every round is a new challenge, every clutch is a chance to become a hero, and every victory feels earned.

What makes Counter-Strike so unique is its simplicity and depth. The mechanics are easy to understand, but mastering them takes countless hours of practice, patience, and dedication. It rewards skill, teamwork, game sense, and the ability to stay calm under pressure.

The feeling of being the last player alive, hearing the bomb ticking, knowing that everything depends on you... There is simply nothing quite like it.

Of course, the game isn't perfect. There are frustrating moments, questionable teammates, cheaters, and matches that make you question your sanity. But somehow, you always find yourself coming back for another game.

And that's the magic of Counter-Strike.

It's not about having the best graphics or the biggest world. It's about the unforgettable moments, the friendships, the rivalries, the intense matches, and the memories you create along the way.

Some games entertain you for a few hours. Counter-Strike gives you memories that last for years.

No matter how many times you uninstall it, somehow, you always come back.

**One more round. Always one more round.**

10/10 — Would recommend. ❤️

review:
CS2 represents a big step visually, but the matchmaking modes are held back by an unchecked cheating problem. For players looking to enjoy standard matchmaking or casual games, it is often an issue of persistent hacking and time waste.

Whether you are queuing for high stakes Competitive/Premier or just want to kick back and relax in Casual, encountering cheaters is an incredibly common experience blatant cheating from subtle wallhacks to blatant 'rage-hacking' (players spinning around and jumping and head shotting everyone they can see), the competitive integrity of the game is deeply compromised.

Casual in CS2 = Bot-Filled, they're always flooded with bots spamming Chinese dating or gambling links. Both teams end up with 2–3 of them, and if it’s not bots, it’s wallhackers or spinbotters — sometimes both. I try to play around 2–3 AM (SEA timezone), and the first match I get in to: bots huddled in a corner, and if you shoot them, they kick you out. It’s ridiculous. Sometimes, this even stretches for like two or a few more matches then I decide to give up and type quit or disconnect on the console.
 
The Mid-Match Cancellation Problem
One of the most infuriating flaws in CS2's anti-cheat implementation (VACNet / Valve Anti-Cheat) is when it decides to respond.

• Wasted Time: Rather than catching and banning a hacker in the opening rounds, the live match moderation often flags the cheater only after you have spent 30 to 40 minutes fighting an uphill battle.
• Uncontinued Matches: When the game finally cancels the match near the very end, it grants zero progress. You are left facing a canceled match with no compensation for your effort, and an hour of your evening completely thrown away.
The Paywall Pressure: Forced to Buy Prime
The competitive ecosystem is explicitly structured to pressure players to spend money, creating a frustrating barrier for those trying out the free-to-play version.

review:
This game needs a 5GB shader update every time I try to launch it. Steam only seems to want to run that update as I launch the game, so I can't play right away. I'll play something else.

I do not recommend this game if you plan on playing vs bots. If you want to jump straight into PVP, expect a high skill floor you'll need to reach before you'll have fun. The support for play against bots is almost non-existent. There is no GUI in game for setting up a custom match vs bots.

Counter-Strike 2 is focused on Player vs Player combat. For a brand new player, facing bots for practice is a good idea, but there is no in game way to change the difficulty level of bots. Bots by default are very easy, and I don't think they'll offer a new player quality practice.

To change the difficulty of bots, you must use the developer console during a match. The multiple commands you need are a bit convoluted. You'll likely need to look up a guide to know what order to use what commands. I didn't have luck getting the commands to work, and I probably did something out of order, or did not remove and re-add the bots at the right time.

There is another console command that can restart the match after you've wasted rounds entering commands, but why is this so difficult? I found my FPS go from 75 to 13 if I opened my web browser, and my FPS did not go above 25 until I restarted the game if I opened and closed my web browser at all while the game was running.

Powered by the Source 2 engine, the game introduces impressive technical upgrades like dynamic volumetric smoke grenades and sub-tick architecture, but the punishingly intense, hacker-infested matchmaking loop fosters deep isolation, leading to a sedentary routine where you gain massive amounts of weight and chain-smoke cigarettes in the dark just to cope with the mounting frustration of a broken game. This hyper-focused digital grind easily spirals into a profound sense of depression and a desperate longing for real human love, yet the crushing loneliness and unfair matches drive you to seek a distorted form of connection through the game's anonymous voice chat, where spending an hour of your time aggressively throwing out racial slurs and calling your teammates the N-word becomes a provocative defense mechanism to assert control and force a reaction when genuine empathy feels entirely out of reach. Ultimately, the high-pressure environment of CS2 offers the ultimate competitive escape, but between the toxic lobbies and the completely useless anti-cheat, it serves as a dark, unplayable refuge that mirrors and worsens personal struggles when real-world fulfillment disappears completely. I would 100% recommend this game.
