review:
CS2 is a display of Valve’s sins and that only gets more true with time. They hijacked the original listing, making the game start off with an “overwhelmingly positive” when that certainly wasn’t the case. This “new” game depending on how you view the previous fiasco is a regression in almost every single aspect excluding polygons. Maps removed, game modes erased, and mechanics broken, surf was broken for literally the longest time. The games art direction has gone from atmospheric to “every corner must be lit up like the sun is throwing a tantrum” for the sake of an e-sports scene that remembers bluer waters. There are more cheaters than ever to the point its impossible to just play a game normally. CSGO used to run on a potato and have functioning anti cheat, and somehow we have lost that. And then there are the BLATANT anti consumer practices from the pro consumer brand. The skins and the ecosystem surrounding it. Skins for the longest time have been distributed in literal gambling crates and this was a game that children played. Furthermore, Valve abuses the artificial scarcity of their skins while having complete control of the market of which they are exclusively sold in. While STILL taking a cut of all second hand sales. They literally caused a 2 billion dollar market crash over a rule change that only served to give them MORE control. This game is more optimized for money than the players and if this had an EA badge on it we would all collectively do the eye roll charade because EA. But this is valve, which makes it even worse, its slimy, grimy and most of all scummy. I understand why Valve has so much good will, they did a lot of work to earn it back in the days of 2013 for some reason. But they are cashing in those checks hard and relying on us to look the other way. We get it you made the play button actually mean something. But this game has degraded to a point where i only use it as a “does this game work well on Linux” test but i can’t even do that anymore cause the install is 80+GB. Furthermore it took the “Linux gaming” company forever to make a Linux native client that for some reason didn’t support steam VR correctly. Just because you make a ton of git commits to the proton repo doesn’t excuse you from this debauchery.

this has moved on from sad to disheartening because i know that the same man that said “just because this is realistic doesn’t mean its fun” is still running this company. Gabe, get off your ass that’s sitting in your yacht, and stand up for the same thing that you stood up for all those years ago. Or do the right thing and pass on the crown to someone else who gives enough of a damn to not be addicted to the gambling money nectar. I’m comparing this company more and more to google rather than Arizona ice tea.

review:
Dear Steam Support Team,

I am writing to request a refund for Counter-Strike 2 because of the extremely frustrating experience I have had with the game, particularly due to the widespread presence of cheaters in matchmaking.

I purchased and played Counter-Strike 2 expecting a competitive first-person shooter where skill, teamwork, aim, and strategy determine the outcome of a match. Unfortunately, my experience has been far from what I expected. Instead of enjoying fair and competitive games, I have repeatedly encountered suspicious players who appear to use cheats, making matches frustrating and, in many cases, completely unenjoyable.

The situation has reached a point where it is difficult to enjoy the game without questioning whether opponents are playing legitimately. Competitive matchmaking should reward players who invest time in improving their skills, learning maps, practicing aim, and working with their teammates. When players appear to gain unfair advantages through cheating, all that effort feels pointless.

What makes this particularly disappointing is the impact on the entire community. Every match affected by suspected cheating wastes the time of legitimate players who simply want to enjoy a fair game. Losing against an opponent who appears to have an unfair advantage is frustrating, but the bigger problem is the loss of trust in the competitive system itself. Players should not have to constantly wonder whether an opponent's performance is legitimate.

Counter-Strike 2 is supposed to be a competitive game, but competitive integrity means very little if players cannot trust the environment in which they are playing. Matchmaking should provide a reasonable level of confidence that everyone is following the same rules. When cheating becomes a recurring concern, the experience loses its value, and players become discouraged from continuing to play.

I understand that detecting and preventing every instance of cheating in an online game is difficult. However, this does not change the fact that players expect meaningful anti-cheat protection and effective action against accounts that break the rules. It is extremely disappointing to spend time playing a game only to feel that fair competition is no longer guaranteed.

The repeated frustration has significantly reduced my enjoyment of Counter-Strike 2. Rather than feeling motivated to improve and continue playing, I increasingly feel that my time is being wasted. I do not believe legitimate players should have to tolerate an experience that consistently falls short of reasonable expectations for a competitive multiplayer game.

For these reasons, I would like Steam Support to review my refund request. I understand that refunds are subject to Steam's refund policy, but I would appreciate consideration of the circumstances and the impact that the recurring cheating problem has had on my experience.

I am disappointed that a game with such a strong competitive reputation has left me feeling this way. I hope that Valve will continue improving its anti-cheat systems and take the concerns of legitimate players seriously. A competitive game can only maintain a healthy community when players have confidence that matches are fair.

Thank you for taking the time to read and review my request. I would appreciate a response regarding my refund eligibility and the options available to me.

Sincerely,
A disappointed Counter-Strike 2 player

Edit 20261018 - The cheats are even more obvious now. only took a week, probably less than the update. My assumption is that the system they are using disproportionately looks at pre aim, and maybe a few other things.  Now you get 5 stacks (that aren't 5 stacks, but they are all cheating together somehow) of cheaters, and a few of them aim at the sky before using the most horrendous aimbot you've ever seen. Then they purposefully try to die to lower their score. and you are held captive in premier, unable to surrender.

Original Post:

This is the best 5v5 competitive tactical shooter. You will feel pain when you first play. Watch a few quick videos on movement and recoil to understand the difference from your simpler shooters. 

"Prime matchmaking" -- Buy Prime. you will have less cheaters, especially as a new player. I bought this game before it was free, so I automatically have "prime account status"

As a new player - don't get discouraged by the 'casual' game mode. I think the max amount of players in casual should be brought down a LOT - the game is best played with smaller servers.

The changes to the premier system I think are good, and will help keep premier from being the same two maps every time. I think Mirage should probably be taken out of the pool, and or Dust 2 (although dust is kind of part of CS's identity). 

The Rush game mode is a breath of fresh air. Good way to warm up, smaller time commitment. Fast paced (as the name suggests) and gets the adrenaline going.

I want to avoid commenting on third party matchmaking like FaceIt, as I have not partaken.

Some quirks/problems:

-Movement feels ever so slightly floaty and slightly heavy at the same time compared to GO - probably an initial acceleration value difference.

-The add for jumpthrows is really nice, but I think could be implemented better. The way it works has a slight delay to check if you made a jump throw or regular throw... as in: if you start moving immediately after your throw, it will affect the throw. This, paired with what feels like a longer delay upon taking out a nade to throw it, makes the game feel slow and unresponsive - and additionally punishes people who have gotten good enough to throw several nades and move in rapid succession. It makes them have to move slower. I think a 'better' solution would be to have a jumpthrow bind in the keybinding menu, and remove this check, but I understand that the layman finds this easier. I do like the sound que that lets you know you successfully made a jumpthrow. 

-Some of the maps wall hitboxes should probably be flattened more in some areas (looking at anything with bricks) for an easier to understand geometry for newer players throwing things like flashbangs (if they hit that one tiny brick on the wall and flash their team more often than not, they may not have the best time? My opinion) -- This tends to happen over time in small updates, not a major problem.

-They're still working on anti-cheat... also, really need a fix to permanently get rid of farming bots. But this is a problem in most multiplayer games now. As a note: In 3 out of my last ~50 games, the game was cancelled due to Vac Live banning someone who we had already figured out was cheating [this is awesome] (it's easy to tell when you've played the game a long time and you use your brain). There were another 4~5 games in there where there was someone that was MAYBE cheating, but honestly they were so bad we didn't care to watch the replay to confirm with 100% certainty. I have seen obvious cheaters on my own team in the past, but not recently. - I've gotten a message about a week after reporting people like this that someone I reported got banned. I'd say that reports, if you assume my actual reports were accurate, get about a 3-~40% success rate at getting a ban. Hard to say for sure. I also don't report folks if I'm just suspicious - I usually watch the replay to make sure I'm not just missing something (you can report from the replay)

-The scanning terminals instead of cases are somehow even more predatory. You get to see what you "won" but then you have to pay a much higher price to get it, with FOMO incentivizing you to. They want a higher percentage on skin sales, basically. Valve, we were already gambling. Have a heart.

Counter-Strike 2 – Somewhere along the way, Counter-Strike forgot games are supposed to be fun.

Somewhere along the line, Counter-Strike seems to have forgotten the "fun" part of the competitive shooter equation. Everything has become so focused on competitive play that I never really felt like coming back.

I was always more into the wacky side of Counter-Strike. Maps like Swimming Pool and Gnome Kitchen, Surf servers, Jailbreak, and all the other ridiculous community-made game modes that made the game so much more than just another competitive shooter.

That was the Counter-Strike I loved. Messing around on weird maps, discovering creative game modes, and having fun without every match feeling like an esports tournament.

It feels like Counter-Strike has slowly left those days behind, and somewhere along the way, it left me behind as well.

Not necessarily a bad game, just no longer the game I fell in love with.

I definitely do not recommend this game to anyone.

They expect us to use third-party platforms to get a clean match because they are too lazy to secure their own official servers.
Do not waste your sanity touching official Premier, Competitive, or Wingman modes until Valve builds a functional anti-cheat. Play FACEIT or stay away entirely. 2/10.

Millions of people are quitting this game, blatant cheaters can play multiple ranked games in a row without being VAC-lived, while top-fraggers who don't cheat are falsely cancelled by VACnet on their very first comp match.

[h1]CSGO[/h1]
I bought CSGO in Oct 1, 2014 (CSGO was $30 back then) and played it on and off. I don't have many hours cos of my dookie laptop from a decade ago that couldn't handle CSGO, and also rage quitting when I played on my brother's PC that could run this game lol. This game gave me a gambling addiction as a kid, but I mean that's just every kid who plays this game, not saying I'm special!!! I remember unboxing a gut knife (urban masked FT) and I was so happy, until my account got hacked and the knife was traded off LOL (this happened right before steam implemented 2FA). But my actual gameplay experience was kinda fun, I loved deathmatch and casual, and nobody was toxic until I started playing comp games, where the joke of "Clutch or Kick" was taken VERY literally by silvers. I was kicked because I couldn't clutch a 1v4, and I just gave up on the game for a while. I've played with gold novas who are more chill than most silvers.

[h1]CS2[/h1]
I got back into this game last month, in my opinion CS2 is definitely more beginner-friendly than CSGO. While toxic players are in every competitive game, I've encountered less toxic players here than on CSGO. I LOVE the addition of Follow Recoil, it's very helpful for people trying to learn spray patterns. But CS2 was suggested to me by a friend who was falsely VACnetted on his first comp game of the night (he's 7k premier and silver btw, if you look at his stats he's clearly NOT cheating), wtf happened to manual review of demos like what the Overwatch system did?? What's the point of trying to get better when you're slapped with a 20 hour VAC cooldown for playing good? But the worst part was that I also received the VAC cooldown since I queued with him. CS2's VACnet has produced way more false-flags than CSGO's VAC, and people are saying that the anti-cheat here is better?? HaiX recently put out a video that shows two cheaters playing wingman, and I mean BLATANT hacks like bhopping and jumping headshots with deagles and scouts, and they weren't VAC-lived until the end of their 7th game. The point of an anti-cheat is to detect cheats, not second-hand guess who the cheater is. I don't care how dog💩 I am at CS, I might switch to Faceit if this 💩 keeps happening ([spoiler]which it will lol[/spoiler])

review:
Counter-Strike 2 – A 20+ Year Veteran’s Review

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike since late fall 2002. I fell in love with it immediately and spent weekend after weekend learning the game inside and out. I watched it grow into 1.6 — the version that, for a lot of people my age, still feels like the peak. I put years into it: new teammates, old teammates, LAN events, and countless hours both in and out of my free time because I genuinely loved the game.

When Source came out it was a rough adjustment. I understood that games need to evolve, so I gave it time and eventually got used to it, even while watching the Counter-Strike I originally fell in love with slowly change. Years later, CS:GO arrived. It was nothing like the game I’d known for over a decade, but I kept an open mind and eventually came to enjoy it on its own terms. The problem was that it never stopped changing. Patch after patch, the shift to free-to-play, systems and updates that most long-time players never asked for — the game kept moving further away from what made so many of us fall in love with it in the first place. It felt like it was being slowly buried under its own updates.

CS2 launched and I once again went in with an open mind. What I found was very little meaningful difference from CS:GO. The creative and structural vision that the original Counter-Strike developers had is gone. It feels like the same game is being recycled with a new label, wrapped in more cases, weapon finishes, ranking systems, and monetization layers. At that point I mostly stopped playing regularly. Now I log in maybe once every couple of weeks, sometimes once a month, because it feels like a shell of what I used to know.
I mainly play Dust 2. Because I don’t play often and rarely touch other maps, the ranking system has kept me in Silver for a long time. When I do play I’m usually at the top of the scoreboard. Recently I received a 20-hour VAC cooldown for “irregular gameplay” after using the Scout on Dust 2 during one of the rare days I actually got to play. From what I understand, the new VACNet system is flagging certain movement and weapon usage — including the Scout — as suspicious, even when no cheating is involved.

I’ve known cheaters have been a problem in this series since the beginning. Seeing Valve’s solution start hitting long-time players who simply play the way they’ve always played is a new low. After more than 20 years, this feels like another clear moment where the veteran player base is being pushed further to the side. I’ve been pretty patient with the changes over the years, but getting locked out of the game for a day because I used a Scout on Dust 2 on one of the few times I logged in is a step too far.

I still have a soft spot for Counter-Strike and I’ll probably come back again eventually. But Valve has spent years steadily alienating the players who stuck with the game the longest, and this is one of the clearest examples yet.

CS2 Is a Disappointing Competitive Shooter: A Detailed Review of Why Counter-Strike 2 Is Bad

An opinionated review of Counter-Strike 2 and why it can feel like a downgrade rather than the next step forward for one of the most iconic competitive shooters ever made.
Introduction: A sequel that doesn't feel like enough of an upgrade

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) had enormous expectations to live up to. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) was one of the most successful competitive shooters of all time, with a legendary esports scene, a dedicated player base, a high skill ceiling, and gameplay that rewarded thousands of hours of practice. When Valve announced CS2, players expected a genuine evolution of the formula: better servers, more consistent hit registration, improved anti-cheat, meaningful quality-of-life improvements, and a polished competitive experience.

Instead, CS2 has often felt like a frustrating mixture of familiar gameplay and persistent technical problems. While the transition to the Source 2 engine brought visual improvements, new smoke mechanics, and updated maps, those changes do not automatically make a game better. A competitive shooter needs to feel responsive, consistent, and fair above everything else.

The biggest criticism of CS2 is that it sometimes feels as though the visual presentation received more attention than the fundamental experience of playing the game. When a player loses a gunfight because of questionable hit registration, encounters a suspected cheater, or experiences inconsistent movement, better lighting and prettier maps provide very little comfort.
1. Inconsistent hit registration and frustrating gunfights

One of the most frustrating aspects of CS2 is the feeling that shots do not always connect in the way players expect them to.

Counter-Strike is built around precision. Every bullet matters, particularly when using weapons such as the AK-47, M4A1-S, or AWP. Players spend hundreds of hours learning recoil patterns, crosshair placement, movement timing, and how to peek angles. In a game with such a high skill ceiling, the shooting mechanics need to feel dependable.

However, some players experience situations where they believe they have landed a clean shot, only for the opponent to survive or kill them almost instantly. Other times, they may die after seemingly reaching cover or feel that an opponent's shot connected despite the visual information on their screen suggesting otherwise.

Not every questionable gunfight is necessarily a technical failure. Counter-Strike relies on server-side hit detection, movement mechanics, recoil, and timing, and players can misjudge what happened. Nevertheless, when the experience repeatedly feels inconsistent, it becomes difficult to trust the game's feedback.

This is particularly damaging because shooting is not a secondary mechanic in CS2. It is the entire foundation of the game. If players cannot confidently understand why they won or lost a duel, the competitive experience becomes significantly less satisfying.

The problem: A precision-based shooter cannot afford to make its core mechanic feel unreliable, regardless of how visually impressive it looks.
2. Sub-tick does not eliminate the feeling of inconsistency

One of CS2's major technical changes was its sub-tick input system. The intention was to improve how the game registers actions such as shooting and movement, rather than relying exclusively on the traditional fixed tick boundaries players associated with CS:GO.

In theory, this should have made the game more responsive and accurate. In practice, however, some players continue to report frustrating discrepancies between what they see and what the game registers.

Peeker's advantage, timing differences, latency, interpolation, and the way movement and shooting are presented can all contribute to these experiences. It would be inaccurate to attribute every frustrating death directly to sub-tick, but the system has not stopped players from questioning the consistency of their gunfights.

For a competitive game, perception matters enormously. Players need to feel that their mechanical skill translates reliably into results. When they repeatedly feel that the game is working against their expectations, they lose confidence in the competitive system.

The criticism is not simply that sub-tick is inherently bad. It is that a major technical overhaul should deliver an unmistakable improvement to the player experience, rather than leave so many players debating whether the fundamentals feel better or worse.
3. Cheating remains a major concern

Cheating is one of the most damaging problems any competitive multiplayer game can face, and CS2 is no exception.

Counter-Strike's competitive structure makes cheating especially frustrating. Matches depend on information gathering, positioning, timing, economy management, and individual mechanical skill. A player who uses wallhacks, aim assistance, or other prohibited software can undermine all of those systems at once.

Imagine spending thirty minutes carefully coordinating with teammates, managing your economy, and adapting to the enemy's strategies, only to suspect that an opponent has an unfair advantage. Even if the match is technically winnable, the experience becomes less about strategy and more about questioning whether the competition is legitimate.

The existence of cheating in a game does not automatically mean its developers are doing nothing to combat it. Anti-cheat is an ongoing challenge, and suspicious behavior can sometimes have legitimate explanations. Nevertheless, the perceived prevalence of cheaters can be enough to undermine trust in ranked matchmaking.

Valve's approach to anti-cheat and enforcement has long been a subject of debate among players. When players do not understand how suspicious accounts are detected, how reports are handled, or whether repeat offenders are being removed effectively, confidence in the system suffers.

The problem: Competitive integrity is not an optional feature. If players cannot trust that their opponents are competing fairly, ranks and match victories lose some of their meaning.
4. Matchmaking can be an exhausting experience

CS2's matchmaking can feel less like a competitive environment designed to produce satisfying games and more like a repeated test of patience.

A good matchmaking system should create reasonably balanced matches, account for individual performance over time, and encourage players to improve. In reality, competitive matches can sometimes feel extremely uneven, with large differences in individual skill, teamwork, communication, and experience.

One match may feature coordinated teams that communicate effectively and understand their roles. The next may involve teammates who refuse to cooperate, players who leave early, arguments over minor mistakes, or individuals who give up after losing a few rounds.

Some of this is unavoidable in a team-based game. No matchmaking algorithm can guarantee perfect teammates or eliminate differences in player behavior. But that does not make the experience less frustrating.

The ranking system can also feel discouraging when players struggle to understand their progress. Losing several games in a row can make improvement feel meaningless, particularly when individual performance does not translate into victories.

And because CS2 places so much emphasis on teamwork, one player's mistakes can have a disproportionate impact on an entire match. You can practice your aim, learn utility lineups, improve your positioning, and still lose because your team repeatedly makes poor decisions.

The result is a competitive experience that can feel punishing without always feeling rewarding.
5. Toxicity makes the community difficult to enjoy.

Subject: Serious Concern About Cheating in CS2 – Ruining the Experience for New Players

Dear CS2 Development Team,

I am writing to express my frustration and disappointment with the current state of cheating in Counter-Strike 2.

As a new player trying to get into the game, my experience has been extremely frustrating. It feels like around 70% of the matches I play involve suspicious players, particularly people seemingly using wallhacks (WH) and other cheats.

It's incredibly discouraging to spend time learning the game, improving my aim, understanding maps, and trying to enjoy competitive matches, only to feel like I'm constantly playing against people who have an unfair advantage.

How is a new player supposed to enjoy CS2 or stay motivated to improve when cheating seems so common? It's ruining the competitive experience, destroying fair gameplay, and pushing potential new players away from the game.

I strongly urge the CS2 team to take this issue more seriously by:

Improving the anti-cheat system and cheat detection.
Taking faster action against confirmed cheaters.
Improving the reporting system and follow-up on reports.
Prioritizing fair matchmaking, especially for new players.
Counter-Strike has an incredible legacy, and CS2 has the potential to be one of the best competitive games out there. But without fair matches, none of that matters.

Please don't let cheaters drive away new players before they even get the chance to fall in love with the game.

I genuinely want to enjoy CS2, improve, and become part of the community, but the current experience makes that extremely difficult.

I hope this feedback reaches the right people and leads to meaningful improvements.

Best regards,
A frustrated new CS2 player who genuinely wants to enjoy the game.

review:
As of 2026 the game is more dead than FragPunk and the devs have left the game in favor of development on Deadlock, minus the 30 people assigned to CS2 who clearly either don't play the game or refuse to tell their superiors the true state of the game so long as money is coming in. Updates to the game are added a year or two in advance and then just left ready to patch in when player numbers drop, like the recent 'pet chicken update' which has been ready and stable for ages yet Valve has a habit of making content for seemingly no reason and then they'll just randomly drop it one day when they've decided they need a player boost.

If you're playing NAE or EU this year, even with a perfect reputation and in-game Green Trust Factor, you'll find it's almost impossible to find a game with ten legit players anymore, because cheating is simply ignored, and in-game drops are based on exp that's founded on Rounds Won and not performance. Valve's own mechanics promote cheating to farm as many items as you can from their Weekly Drops or Armory Pass systems. No matter how much the community complains or pro players alert Valve, they don't care, and their previous two "major actions" essentially boiled down to "Half of our player base are now item-farming bots. We should remove the rare and expensive Weekly Drop items" and "The top players in our seasonal leaderboard are all well known hackers and bots. Delete the Leaderboard function from the game". You'll find in these regions VAC is basically useless even when they claim to have a large wave of bans, as Valve's priority seems to be keeping as many Eastern European players as possible, as their poor national states gives rise to gambling and engaging with Valve's systems. I know people on both sides of the Russia/Ukraine war who've taken to cheating and selling accounts because it's a way of making money while their homes go to crap and Valve profits from having "an active playerbase" and players engaging with the market, where they take a cut.

The game functions mostly as a case-opening gambling simulator, but even then the Market is down so badly (roughly 25-50% of stable item prices have been cut off) because legitimate players are a slim fraction of the population now. You'd think now is a good time to buy said items but every day we see more and more players leaving and uninstalling because once you've left and moved on, the sunk cost nonsense goes away. You may as well save your items for the day maybe the game is good, and save your money not buying items for a game you should leave. Valve introduced "a friendlier gambling option" with their Terminal system that's supposed to offer skins at around market price, however the items offered are always cheaper from the market (in better condition too) and are significantly cheaper-for-better on third-party sites (often the price of a beaten up terminal item will get you the same item pristine, or nearly pristine online). These systems exist just to silence government anti-gambling agencies and to get money from countries who cannot use said third-party sites and are relegated to the Steam Community Market. They're not balanced or honest and, like most of the game's practices, exist only to tax the stupid and the 'geographically-handicapped' as Valve would call it.

If you have any maps or skins in the game, which I don't personally but my boyfriend does, you'll likely know that the Workshop function has changed drastically too. Not only are the maps and skins player-made but they're now paid on a fixed-rate basis and not as a percentage of sales. This is fine for mappers as that's a one-and-done thing but for skin creators they've basically nuked 90% of the revenue you would have received (and those older players have received) for a stable palming-off price they can shut you up with, especially as they've not yet removed gambling or cases at all, so previous collections still see their creators paid significantly more. This is fine for anyone who already had work in the game but they're basically asking current and future users to design maps and skins for their game that's already on life support, for little reward, certainly compared to the older, better skin creators, and hoping that nobody asks them questions about their own pay. Older creators still get their monthly pay but anyone getting into it now won't get more than a small cheque and probably not even a thanks.

Events are over. We used to get seasonal events, in-game items, stream rewards, souvenirs, etc. Since CS2 has launched there's been nothing. No Operations, though since the playerbase seems barely legitimate anymore you can understand Valve not making large updates that requires models and voice lines anymore. Even worse though, while the game gets an update every few days to a week, to update coding and allow better Community Updates, there is no CS2 Community. All the major servers and CSGO scenes are gone, and have not, and will not, come back. Sure we have Surf, KZ, and BHop servers, but CSGO had full working ports of all the classic CSS maps and modes. Simpsons Gungame, Decoy Dodgeball, Zombies, Prop Hunt, Lego modes (though 1v1 Lego AWP Arena exists still), Hide and Seek, the various horror modes that weren't just zombie wave maps, kart racing, etc. They're all gone, and most of those communities have stated they're not looking to come back. A big one was UKCS but a bunch of NA community scenes over here all retired their servers after CSGO died. Valve keeps updating the game to make community things easier to make and run but there's nobody left who wants it, and it seems like those updates are to CS2 what Forge was to Halo Infinite. Yeah the toolkit is cool but the game is dead and nobody will ever truly engage with it, besides maybe mappers wanting their easy 30 grand for a game they won't play.


If you don't have the game already, there's better alternatives out there. If you wanna play with bots and maybe revive a better game, go save FragPunk. If you want the CS gameplay with abilities and skins, play Valorant. If you just want simple CS gunplay and a military motif, I can think of at least three superior games on Steam, but also just go back to CS:S. 
The devs don't care about the true state of the game, beyond that it's making them millions monthly. The community scene is all dead outside of a few modes. In-game creators have been shafted because Valve wants as much money as possible before they're forced to remove gambling entirely. There's nothing in CS2 that wasn't either better in Source or Global Offensive, and there's little left in CS that hasn't been done better by companies who don't hate you as much as Valve does. Save yourself the headache and play better.

review:
Genuinely one of the most unfriendly games for new players ive ever tried. I spent several evenings trying to get to grips with this because I liked the idea of drop-in drop-out gameplay with a high skill ceiling that rewarded investment.

I tried deathmatch, only to get head-tapped by AKs with frame-perfect reactions. I read a bit and it turns out deathmatch/casual isnt good because its swarmed by bots running scripts to farm kills for experience and crates. Okay whatever I unlocked competitive, thats like the ranked thing isnt it? So I'll be able to play with people around my skill level? I won maybe one game out of a full fifteen, the one that I won was because the other team literally had a player disconnect, every other game wasn't close either, like blowouts every time. Read some more and it turns out the matchmaking is so poor that most games are completely one-sided, driven by one or two players playing several times better than anyone else farming kills, which was exactly my experience. Okay, dunno why its called competitive then, but someone in one of these games told me Premiere is probably more my speed. Awesome! Oh wait, nevermind, after a literal entire calendar day of playing Im only 30% of the way to unlocking that mode.

Practice isnt the solution, and saying otherwise is an excuse to offload the labor of onboarding new players. Everywhere I look I'm being told to "embrace the suck and practice", but practice modes with bots dont get me out of lobbies full of people that have been playing for a lifetime longer than I have and can hit frame-perfect AWP headshots in their sleep; And telling a new player "it sucks for the first hundred hours then you maybe get kinda good" feels braindead when the market for competitive shooters is as flooded as its ever been. There's a million options that respect my time, why choose the option that feels like it goes out of its way to be hostile?

A functioning match-making system to group the people that can hit frame-perfect AWP headshots and people like me separately shouldnt be beyond this billion-dollar corporation, or the game modes that provide that shouldnt be so separate. You can tell this game has been around for literal generations, and that the average player is a returning player. In loading in for the first time you're inundated with menus (and opportunities to purchase cosmetics, gross), with next to zero real explanation for what anything is. When you're designing a product under the assumption that the average user has been using it for a lifetime already, you dont think about new players. Thats exactly whats happened with this game, and you feel it every hour the game's running. It feels like I'm missing a thousand hours of context before I should even be able to launch.

0/10, will be actively rooting for CS2's downfall

review:
Counter Strike always had been a good game
I started playing 1.6 with my cousin when i was ~5 to 6 years old on zombie mode made by community, Same for counter strike source

I loved watching those videos of players recording themselves playing those gamemodes, it was very entertaining and I am very happy to have Counter Strike as a part of my childhood

Same for csgo that was a banger, i remember hitting a 7vs1 with awp on awp lego servers 
There was this feeling of comfort that Counter Strike 2 will never get

Sure there was a lot of cheaters, this is without any doubt, probably we would see them less often due to the massive amount of game modes, but there was overwatch, an anti-cheat that was not perfect, but did the job, the bhop felt nice, the physic felt nice, animation were smooth and no problem at all

Today, the game is full of cheaters, premier, competitive, rush, wingman, casual every mode includes cheaters at a very high rate

I did not mention cheaters in deathmatch because there isn't a single cheater there, except for bots who their only objective is to farm weekly care package for cases (alias money)

It was so bad that Valve had to remove the good drops (CSGO weapon case 1, 2 and bravo case)

Spinbotters in premier will make you leave the game sooner that you came in, one game you win 150 elo, the next spinbotters that will make you lose between 200 and 450 elo 

Valve is not even doing the skins anymore, or maps, it's just a rotation of community maps, same for game modes and operations

The game lacks of content, and you feel it when Valve adds chickens instead of fixing real problems

Animgraph2 popped up on AK, AWP, SCOUT, M4A4, M4A1-S, and most of them got wiped out for no reason (at least they were not given) when they were nice.

The game's physic is not perfect, when cs2 released it was horribly bad, and was like the player got 50kg added on his body (It got improved today, but it's still not like CSGO)

The optimizations could be done better, same for the storage, at the moment cs2 is about ~75gb if I am not mistaken when CSGO was 35gb MAX (If I am not wrong)

TL:DR :

- Anti cheat needs improvement
- New content needed (Old game modes back, operations or even weapons)
- A better physic for movements like strafe jumps or such
- Better Optimizations (on some animations like pull outs, or even FPS opti)
- Do not touch with people's trust (Random update that makes -2 billion$ on the global market)
- Put the old ban map system on premier
- Put the old point system to 16, and an option for 13 rounds in case people wants short matches
- Fix the Tab bug, when pressing tab the game freezes shortly, or does insane FPS drops (or it gives FPS boost when low FPS for some people)

Thanks for reading all that, sorry for the spelling mistakes (I won't ask slop gpt to correct them)

When the cooldown expired, I gave the game another chance, only to have my very first match disrupted and receive a 7-day cooldown. I have never used cheats, and I even tried closing background applications to rule out potential software conflicts.

Meanwhile, encountering suspected cheaters in actual matches remains frustrating. It feels backwards when legitimate players end up afraid to play because of repeated anti-cheat detections they cannot explain.

I'm not claiming that every VACNET detection is wrong, but legitimate players deserve transparency, a reliable way to appeal potential false positives, and confidence that they won't risk escalating penalties without understanding why.

After receiving repeated cooldowns despite not cheating, I no longer feel comfortable playing CS2. I don't want to risk a permanent VAC ban over something I haven't done.

Until Valve addresses these concerns and provides a clearer process for affected players, I cannot recommend CS2 to anyone who values their account and competitive experience.

I absolutely LOVE Counter-Strike 2. ...So why don't I recommend it?

I think it's a great game, considering the rough start after CS:GO. However, over time, especially within the last few months, I noticed I wasn't playing Counter-Strike 2 anymore - it didn't even felt like I was playing any kind of Counter-Strike. Why? Ever since Counter-Strike: Global Offensive became Counter-Strike: Gambling Objective, I was already not experiencing the Counter-Strike game I grew up with. 

Before the skins and gambling, CS actually felt like a very competitive skill game. The amount of so called content creators on YouTube that actually create multiple full length video's each week about new skins and changes etc. really made me realize that CS:GO, and now CS2 had became a casual FPS game that has now reached a whole extra audience that only care about digital pixels. With these skins and stuff, I feel it's more about the inventory than it is about the actual skill. 

But this wasn't my biggest concern, and not the reason I do not recommend this game. I almost never write reviews, but as they say in elections, every vote counts, ..this is my vote. Although it's just one simple man's opinion, this game is not playable or enjoyable any longer due to the amount of cheaters  in this game. The situation has became really, really bad. To every dedicated player that made it this far in my review, thank you, please consider writing a review yourself as a signal to Valve to let them know that we are fed up with the lack of attention to this matter. 

Peace.
